nameStory: The white Atlantic cadlina gets its straightforward name from its pristine white coloration and its home in Atlantic waters. The genus name 'Cadlina' honors the Italian naturalist Cadlina, though the 'laevis' part means 'smooth' in Latin, describing this sea slug's sleek, polished appearance.
description: The white Atlantic cadlina is a sea slug - specifically a nudibranch, which means 'naked gills' - that has abandoned the typical snail shell for a soft, flexible body. These marine creatures look like tiny underwater gems, with a smooth, translucent white body that can appear almost ghostly as they glide across underwater surfaces. As dorid nudibranchs, they have their gills arranged in a flower-like cluster on their back end. They're relatively small creatures, typically measuring just a few centimeters in length.

idTips.label: Pure white coloration
idTips.description: The body is distinctively pure white or translucent white, often with a slightly pearlescent quality that catches light underwater like frosted glass

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: The body surface feels smooth and slippery to gentle touch, lacking the bumps, ridges, or projections found on many other sea slugs

idTips.label: Gill arrangement
idTips.description: Look for a circular cluster of feathery gills at the rear end of the body, arranged like the petals of a small flower

idTips.label: Rhinophores
idTips.description: Two club-shaped sensory organs stick up from the head like tiny periscopes, often with a slightly wrinkled or laminated surface

idTips.label: Gliding movement
idTips.description: Moves with a characteristic smooth, flowing glide across surfaces, leaving no visible slime trail behind

habitat: White Atlantic cadlinas are found in New England's cold marine waters, typically on rocky subtidal areas and kelp forests from the low tide zone down to deeper waters. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often found grazing on encrusting sponges that grow on rocks, pier pilings, and kelp holdfasts. You're most likely to spot them while snorkeling or diving in rocky coastal areas from Maine to Cape Cod.

seasonality.spring: More active as water temperatures begin to rise, making this a good time for divers to spot them moving across rocky surfaces and sponge colonies.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible and active, feeding extensively on sponges in warmer water temperatures.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down as water temperatures drop, though they remain visible to divers in their typical rocky habitats.
seasonality.winter: Less active in cold water but still present, moving more slowly and staying closer to their sponge food sources on protected rocky surfaces.

funFact: White Atlantic cadlinas are living chemical laboratories that steal defensive compounds from the sponges they eat, incorporating these toxins into their own bodies to make themselves unpalatable to predators - essentially turning their dinner into their bodyguard!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other white sea slugs or even small white anemones when the gills are retracted, but the smooth gliding movement and distinctive gill flower when extended are dead giveaways - remember 'smooth mover with a flower power' for this species.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills,' referring to the exposed, unprotected gills that these sea slugs wear on the outside of their bodies like external lungs. Don't confuse these marine nudibranchs with terrestrial slugs - they're completely different creatures that just happen to share a similar soft-bodied, shell-less appearance.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cadlina species recorded in New England waters, compare it with other white dorid nudibranchs in the region. Unlike many relatives, the white Atlantic cadlina maintains its pure white coloration and completely smooth body surface, while other white sea slugs often have spots, ridges, or colorful markings that break up their white appearance.
